title: Nanotechnology in Medicine (Awareness Level)
desc: Understand how very small materials are used in medicine, from imaging to drug delivery, and how safety, testing and ethics apply. Awareness only.
outcomes: Explain what nanoscale means and give three medical uses.
Use size comparisons and units correctly.
Compare benefits and risks of nanomedicines.
Judge claims in news and adverts.
task: Write a two-page briefing on three medical uses of nanotechnology, with benefits, risks, evidence stage and ethical questions.
condition: A computer, public information, two peers and a mentor. No laboratory work is done in this course.
standard: Units and sizes are correct; each use has an evidence stage; risks are stated; no overclaims; sources dated; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Science students, biomedical trainees, health writers, regulators' assistants.
modules: A nanometre is one billionth of a metre.
A hair is about 80,000 nm wide; a virus about 100 nm.
Materials behave differently at this size.
Gold looks red when particles are tiny, not yellow.
Make a size chart from hair to atom.
Tiny particles can make signals clearer.
Contrast agents and rapid test strips use nanoparticles.
Sensors can detect small amounts of a marker.
False results still occur; follow-up tests are needed.
A rapid test shows a coloured line using gold particles.
Explain a test strip in your own words.
Carriers can protect a drug and aim it.
Lipid particles carry some vaccines and drugs.
The body can clear or react to carriers.
Fat-based particles shield fragile genetic material during delivery.
Size, shape and surface decide where they travel.
Liver and kidneys clear many particles.
Particles above a certain size stay in the liver longer.
Make a table of size and body route.
Lab, animal-free methods where possible, human trials, approval.
Regulators ask for size distribution, stability and safety.
A batch is rejected because particle size varied.
Map the path from lab to patient.
Environmental release during manufacture and disposal.
A plant uses closed systems and masks for powders.
Check evidence stage: idea, lab, trial, approved.
A news story calls a lab result a cure; the learner marks it "lab stage".
The reader can explain why approval takes years.
quiz: How many nanometres in a metre?
Imaging, test strips or drug delivery.
Why does size matter in the body?
It decides where particles go and how they clear.
rubric: Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others
next: DNA analysis, stem cells, materials science basics.
ladder: L1: learner can say what nano means.
L2: learner can name medical uses.
L3: learner can read size charts.
L4: learner can explain delivery and clearance.
L5: learner can review claims and regulation.
L6: learner can coordinate a lab file.
L7: learner can audit a briefing.
